title: How To Test Your Class Rules
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a simple diagnostic exercise for testing whether a class's rules truly cover every possible disruption. Teachers draw a square representing a well-behaved classroom, then list every misbehavior they've witnessed outside it, checking each against their current rules and underlining any that aren't clearly covered. Underlined items represent gaps, or 'openings in the wall,' that will widen into recurring problems if left unaddressed. The exercise's larger purpose is to eliminate gray areas so that both teacher and students know precisely which behaviors trigger which rule, which in turn makes consistent enforcement dramatically easier and prevents the arguments, confusion, and lost respect that ambiguous rules invite.
points: Introduces a square-diagram exercise: list all past misbehaviors outside a square representing a well-behaved class, then match each to an existing rule.
Behaviors that can't be matched to a rule are underlined as 'openings' that will widen into recurring misbehavior if unaddressed.
Teachers must decide whether each gap can fold under an existing rule or requires a new one.
The exercise's core purpose is eliminating gray areas so teacher and students agree exactly which misbehavior triggers which rule.
Clear, gap-free rules are framed as the foundation for consistent, confident enforcement and avoiding arguments and wishy-washy appearances.
quotes: It’s to form an impenetrable boundary that keeps misbehavior out and the freedom to teach in.
Outside of the square, write down every misbehavior you can think of that you’ve witnessed in the past five years—or for as long as you’ve been teaching.
The underlined behaviors are openings in your wall. They result in guaranteed confusion—for both you and your students—more misbehavior, and slower academic progress.
This is critical because when you’re able to recognize rule-breaking when you see it—i.e. no gray areas —then being consistent in enforcing consequences becomes a lot easier.
You avoid the loopholes and frustration of seeing the same misbehavior repeated again and again.
You also avoid appearing wishy-washy and losing respect and influence.
